playbook:
I treat it as a stock-building problem until the final round, then as a liquidation problem.

- When 2+ seasons remain, I set catch = the displayed sustainable share, rounded to one decimal. No tilt, no "making up ground."
- When one rival repeatedly lands slightly above the share (in this run boat 1 held ~13.0–13.5 throughout), I don't chase; I anchor on the share and add at most a small premium (~10%) for one or two mid seasons, then return to the share. The rival's overage is small enough that regrowth absorbs it — the stock only drifted 100 → 78 over five seasons, never near danger.
- When the other rival lands at or below the share (boat 2 drifted 11.1 → 10.8 → 10.0 → 8.5 → 9.3), that's a signal the pool is not being contested mid-game; no premium is needed and under-share catches by others are free regrowth for my final round.
- When total landed = share for everyone, I keep the cadence and let regrowth do the scoring. A +3 mid-season grab costs roughly the same in lost regrowth and signals escalation.
- If the stock gets meaningfully below ~60 before the end, I tighten to slightly under the share so the last-round stock stays worth harvesting.
- Entering the final season, I switch objective to clearing the pool: estimate each rival's final bid from their recent trend (here ~13 and ~9.3, total ~22.5) and bid (remaining stock − expected rival take − small buffer). With 78.3 on the table I bid 53 and landed it — the formula beat the old episode's smaller pool exactly as designed. Key check: my bid must leave the stock non-negative after rounding, and should leave at most their expected take behind. If rivals have been consistently greedy, shave the buffer; if passive, take a bit less than the max.
- Don't overthink mid-season messages: one-line arithmetic, end on the bracket token. No confessions, no extra market talk.

1.text:
When the game opens with a regenerating shared resource, I commit to harvesting at or just above the sustainable share — the regrowth math makes conservation the dominant strategy for total score, not a moral choice. A small premium (1–2 fish over the share) from season 1 is safe and free value when the stock is at or near cap.

Before each submission I do the quick arithmetic: current stock, post-harvest regrowth, seasons remaining. I never take an amount that, combined with plausible rival takes, would push the stock toward zero — collapse is the only outcome that ruins me regardless of my relative position.

When I'm behind on total score, I increase my take modestly (roughly 1.2–1.5x the sustainable share), not aggressively. I size my aggression to what the stock can survive even if others grab too.

When I'm ahead, I defend by fishing at the sustainable share or a small premium above it — there's no reason to risk collapse to widen a lead, and restraint pulls rivals toward restraint too.

I watch the landed history for each rival's pattern. Rivals stable at or near the sustainable share tell me the stock will hold, so I can safely take a small premium every mid-game season. If a rival trends downward over time (e.g. 11 → 10.5 → 9.3, suggestively close to tracking the sustainable share), I treat them as a share-tracker and expect them to be even more conservative later — useful info for the final-season grab. If a rival spikes hard, I don't match — I wait for them to settle before pressing my own premium.

Through the middle seasons I bank a consistent small premium (share plus 2–4) rather than alternating restraint and spikes — against cooperative rivals this accumulates a lead without ever testing the stock. This works: holding a steady 13–13.5 while rivals took 8.5–13 left me level or slightly ahead going into the finale.

I go heavy only when the endgame makes regrowth irrelevant: in the final season there is no future to protect, so I take as much as the stock minus expected rival takes allows. The improved sizing from last time paid off — taking 45 from a 78 stock against rivals landing ~9–13 each was safe. To tighten further: subtract rivals' modal recent take (not their maximum) unless a rival has shown spiking behaviour, and take the full remainder once I know the boats submit independently (the harbour records the figure submitted, so there's no claim mechanism to overshoot). Against share-trackers, even stock minus ~25 would have been safe; I left ~76 fish of total stock on the table by rounding down to 45. Frame it explicitly: final take = stock − (sum of each rival's typical recent take) − small buffer.

If the first season's history line shows fewer entries than rival boats, don't over-read formatting quirks — infer rival behaviour only from complete seasons.

I keep any reasoning in my reply short and always end with the required bracketed token.

2.text:
- When a season opens, I first compute the safe default: the stated sustainable share (roughly stock plus regrowth, divided by boats). That is my anchor every season, not my opening bid.
- In the first season, when no one has revealed a style yet, I do NOT spike. I take exactly the sustainable share — not even a notch above. Bank information, not fish.
- When other boats take the sustainable share, I take the sustainable share. Matched restraint keeps the regrowth base large, and the flowing payoff exceeds any one-season grab.
- I read rivals from season 1, not just late. This game boat 3 overshot (~13) every single season from the start — there was no cooperative track record to trust and then lose. Classify each boat by season 2: at-share, small premium, or persistent grabber, and plan around the persistent grabber being a permanent feature.
- I track the total take, not just my own. The break-even is total catch equal to regrowth. Here total take ran ~34–35 against a falling break-even, so the stock slid 100 → 78.3 across six seasons even though two boats were "reasonable."
- Unilateral restraint has limits. I cut below share (10.0, 8.5) and the stock still fell because the grabber didn't respond. I still make one visible 10–15% cut as a signal, but if the grabber doesn't match within a season, I stop donating fish: I hold at exact share and shift my edge to the terminal haul. A survivor in a live fishery beats a leader in a dead one — but a saint feeding a grabber just loses.
- With a persistent grabber in the pool, treat sustainability as already lost and optimize timing: the question becomes when to take, not whether to conserve. The fishery will not recover; every season I stay at share while they grab, my relative position worsens.
- Rivals may still defect late even after restraint. From season N-1 onward I assume someone will grab, and I make my terminal plan one season early.
- I never take a large grab before the final season unless the stock is heading to zero regardless of what I do. Spikes signal aggression and invite a scramble. My season-5 hold at 9.3 was right: stock was still 83.8, and grabbing early only drags the terminal stock down for everyone.
- In the final season, with no future to protect: take a disciplined terminal haul around a third of the stock when others are likely to grab too — not the naive maximum, and certainly not the sustainable share. My 25 from 78.3 was right again; taking 8.7 would have donated ~16 points to the grabber.
- I size any non-final premium small (at most ~10% above share, and only while total take stays below break-even and the stock is stable or rising). If those conditions fail, I revert to at-or-below share immediately.
- What did not work: tiny premiums stacked on other boats' overshoots, and repeated small cuts that nobody matched. My edge comes from an accurate read of aggregate take plus a well-timed terminal haul, not from being permanently the "+1" boat or the "-1" boat.
- Each decision, I ask in order: Is this season N? Terminal haul, ~one third of stock. N-1? Hold share, pre-commit to the terminal number now. Otherwise, is total take at or below break-even? Then hold at share. If not, cut once as a signal, then hold at share and bank on the finish.
